title: 10 Frameworks to Eliminate Invisible Drag
author: Vicky Zhao
summary: The companion PDF to Vicky Zhao's invisible-drag video, holding all ten traps where the video covered only two. Each is the same shape: a word or concept that carries more than one meaning, the trap it creates when nobody notices, and a named framework for splitting it. The underlying claim is that most disagreement at work is not disagreement at all — it is two people using one label for different realities, agreeing out loud and diverging in the work.
takeaways: 1. TIME HORIZON — same word, different timeframes. 'Efficiency' means finishing today's task faster, or building a system that saves time weekly. Ask: immediate results, durable results, or both?
2. LEVELS OF ANALYSIS — a person-level, team-level and org-level issue discussed as one thing. Ask at what level the problem is actually happening, so you do not solve the wrong layer.
3. 5W1H — take a vague word and ask how its meaning changes across Who, What, When, Where, Why, How. 'Fast' changes by when: fast to start versus fast to finish.
4. MEANS VS ENDS — defending an approach as if it were the outcome. Ask: is this the objective, or one possible route to it? Stops teams mistaking activity for progress.
5. INPUT / PROCESS / OUTPUT / OUTCOME — 'not working' means poor inputs to one person, bad execution to another, weak impact to a third. Locate where the drag sits before fixing it.
6. STAKEHOLDER LENS — a decision that is good from one view and bad from another, discussed as if one standard of good exists. Compare how the same action looks to each stakeholder.
7. SURFACE VS STRUCTURE — reacting to symptoms and missing the cause, producing repeated fixes. Repeated missed deadlines look like discipline but may be unclear prioritisation.

8. INSIDE VS OUTSIDE — over-attributing to the person, under-attributing to the environment. Separates skill and judgement from tools, incentives, workload and structure. Creates better design instead of blame.

9. CAPABILITY VS BEHAVIOUR — treating one moment as proof of a permanent gap. Ask: skill gap, or performance gap in context? Someone can have strong communication capability and still handle one tense meeting badly.
10. DESCRIPTIVE VS EVALUATIVE — words that sound precise but are judgements. 'That wasn't professional' becomes 'you interrupted twice and did not answer the client's question directly'.
quotes: People use the same word while optimizing for different timeframes... The disagreement stays invisible because both sound reasonable.
A concept feels blurry because nobody has tested it from enough angles. People use one label for many different realities because they have not broken the situation apart.
Teams say something is 'not working,' but they are talking about different parts of the chain.
People over-attribute problems to the person and under-attribute them to the environment. This creates blame instead of better design.
People use words that sound precise but are really judgments. Terms like 'strategic,' 'professional,' or 'good leadership' often carry approval without enough description.
bestIdeas: Descriptive vs evaluative is the most immediately usable. Converting a judgement into observable behaviour is the difference between feedback someone can act on and feedback they can only resent.
Inside vs outside reframes performance conversations as design problems. 'Blame instead of better design' names exactly what goes wrong when the environment is not considered.
Input/process/output/outcome gives a shared vocabulary for 'it's not working', which is otherwise the least actionable sentence in any review.
Surface vs structure is systems thinking in one question, and pairs directly with the iceberg model already in the vault.
5W1H is already one of Dom's own mental models in TELOS — here it is repurposed as a disambiguation tool rather than an analysis one, which is a genuinely different use.
tools: The PDF itself: `Attachments/10 Frameworks to Eliminate Invisible Drag — Vicky Zhao.pdf` (44MB, 11 pages).
method: Spot the load-bearing word before agreement is reached.

Pick the framework matching the kind of ambiguity: timeframe (1), altitude (2), general vagueness (3), goal vs route (4), stage of the chain (5), whose view (6), symptom vs cause (7), person vs system (8), can vs did (9), fact vs judgement (10).
Split the concept using that framework and state both halves for the room.
The video's two-part split is the delivery mechanism: say what you do NOT mean, then what you do.

keyMessage: Most workplace disagreement is not disagreement — it is one label covering different realities, so name which kind of ambiguity you are facing and split the concept before the work starts.
